knitr::opts_chunk$set(

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(dyadMLM)
library(dplyr)
has_glmmTMB <- requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)
```

Dyadic samples often include people observed without their partner. Some
have no partner (singles, widowed people). Others have a partner who did not
take part. In longitudinal studies, people can also lose or gain a partner.
This vignette shows how to keep all of them in a dyadic multilevel model with
the `partner_exists` argument of `prepare_dyad_data()`.

It builds on the
[Actor-Partner Interdependence Model vignette](apim.html), in particular its
[exchangeable residual structure](apim.html#exchangeable-residual-structure)
with a shared and a member-contrast term. The models use `glmmTMB`. For
`brms`, see the backend note in `?recover_exchangeable_covariance`.

## Record whether a partner exists

By default, `prepare_dyad_data()` stops when a dyad has only one person in
the data, because it cannot tell whether that person's partner exists.
`incomplete_dyads = "drop"` removes these people instead. In longitudinal
data, a partner who has a row at some occasions is assumed to exist at all
occasions of the dyad, with missing values where their row is missing.

`partner_exists` records whether a partner exists. It is `TRUE` or `FALSE`
for everyone observed alone (the only person of their dyad in the data,
across all occasions), or a column (or expression) with a value for each
row. People observed alone get their own label (`.composition`) and
indicator column (`.is_*`):

| Situation | `partner_exists` | Label with `role` | Label without `role` | Partner predictors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Partner did not take part | `TRUE` | `<role>_x_missing` | `missing_partner` | missing (`NA`) |
| No partner at any observed occasion (*singleton*) | `FALSE` | `singleton_<role>` | `singleton` | 0 |
| Partner lost or gained during the study | `TRUE` while a partner exists | dyad label, e.g., `female_x_male` | `assumed_exchangeable` | 0 where no partner exists |

- A label stays the same across occasions. A person observed alone who had a
  partner at some occasion is labeled as having a partner who did not take
  part.
- Base `partner_exists` on recorded status, such as relationship status or
  widowhood, not on whether both people supplied data. A rule such as
  `dplyr::n() == 2` mixes the two kinds of people observed alone.
- Give each singleton their own `dyad` ID, never a shared ID or `NA`.
- Where both members have a row at an occasion, their values must agree.
  After a separation in which both keep taking part, both are `FALSE`.

## Partners who did not take part

Where a partner exists but has no row, their values are missing, like any
other missing data. People whose partner did not take part keep their rows,
so models can use their outcomes [@knaflCrossSectionalFamilyDyads2009].
Models with partner predictors drop these rows (listwise deletion), while
actor-only models keep them. In actor-only models, they can share a mean with
dyad members, for example with `I(.is_male + .is_male_x_missing)`. Check
`nobs()`, and compare results with and without these people, for example in
an actor-only model. An appropriate dyadic imputation model can retain them
under a plausible missing-at-random assumption.

The same applies in longitudinal data. For example, with
`partner_exists = TRUE`, a person whose partner never took part is labeled
`missing_partner` and keeps their rows for actor-only models. Nothing is set
to 0.

When reporting, count the rows left out only because the partner predictor
is missing (here with placeholder column names):

```{r report-missing-partners, eval = FALSE}
left_out <- is.na(data$.x_gmc_partner) &
  !is.na(data$outcome) & !is.na(data$.x_gmc_actor)
sum(left_out)                              # n rows
dplyr::n_distinct(data$personID[left_out]) # from m people
```

For example: "*n* rows from *m* people had missing partner predictors. They
were retained for centering and excluded from models including those
predictors."

## Two-part partner predictors

Where no partner exists, a partner value is not missing but undefined. To
keep these rows, `prepare_dyad_data()` uses the two-part predictors of
@dziakTwoPartPredictors2017 (Method 1), which also work with repeated
observations [@henryTwoPartFatherChild2022]. After centering, partner
predictors are set to 0 where no partner exists, and `.partner_exists`
(1 or 0) marks these rows. `.partner_exists` is only created when the status
varies.

Include `.partner_exists` as a fixed effect, so that rows without a partner
get their own mean. Otherwise, the zeros are treated as real partner values,
which can bias the partner effects. Random effects cannot replace it. It can
be left out only if fixed intercepts already separate the rows without a
partner, for example singleton indicators when only singletons lack a partner.

With centered actor and partner scores $x_A$ and $x_P$, the fixed means are:

$$
\mu =
\begin{cases}
\beta_0 + \beta_A x_A, & \text{without a partner}, \\
\beta_0 + \beta_S + \beta_A x_A + \beta_P x_P,
  & \text{with a partner}.
\end{cases}
$$

The status coefficient $\beta_S$ compares people with and without a partner
at equal actor scores, when the partner score equals its centering reference.
It is not "the effect of having a partner". The partner slope applies to
people with a partner. The actor slope is shared.

## Cross-sectional data: singletons and complete dyads

Complete dyads and singletons can share one model. Singletons then inform
the shared effects, such as the actor slope, while complete dyads also inform
the partner effect and the dependence between partners. Estimation can be
less reliable with few complete dyads and many people observed alone
[@duNumberDyadsEstimation2016].

For this example, we simulate closeness from the support scores in
`dyads_cross`, with one observation per person. Each composition
(female-male, female-female, and male-male) has 80 complete dyads and 40
singletons (`has_partner = 0`). The simulated actor slope is 0.6 and the
partner slope is 0.3. Singletons and dyad members of the same gender have the
same residual variance.

```{r simulate-cross-sectional, include = FALSE}
set.seed(20261001)
solo_source <- dyads_cross |>
  group_by(coupleID) |>
  mutate(
    source_composition = paste(sort(as.character(gender)), collapse = "_x_"),
    partner_support = rev(provided_support),
    shared_error = rnorm(1, sd = 0.6)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

singleton_clusters <- solo_source |>
  distinct(coupleID, source_composition) |>
  group_by(source_composition) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 1 / 3) |>
  ungroup()

removed_members <- solo_source |>
  semi_join(singleton_clusters, by = "coupleID") |>
  group_by(coupleID) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

cross_sample <- solo_source |>
  anti_join(removed_members, by = "personID") |>
  mutate(
    has_partner = as.integer(!coupleID %in% singleton_clusters$coupleID),
    closeness = 3 + 0.4 * (gender == "female") + 0.3 * has_partner +
      0.6 * (provided_support - 5) +
      0.3 * ifelse(has_partner == 1, partner_support - 5, 0) +
      shared_error + rnorm(n(), sd = ifelse(gender == "female", 0.8, 1))
  )

select_columns <- function(data) {
  select(data, personID, coupleID, gender, has_partner, closeness, provided_support)
}
mm_raw <- select_columns(filter(cross_sample, source_composition == "male_x_male"))
fm_raw <- select_columns(filter(cross_sample, source_composition == "female_x_male"))
```

### Prepare the data

`mm_raw` holds the male-male sample. `coupleID` identifies a complete dyad or
one singleton.

```{r prepare-dyads-and-singletons, message = FALSE}
mm_data <- prepare_dyad_data(
  mm_raw, dyad = coupleID, member = personID, role = gender,
  predictors = provided_support, add_apim_gmc_predictors = TRUE,
  partner_exists = has_partner == 1, seed = 123
)
mm_data
```

The composition table lists 80 male-male dyads and 40 singleton men.
Singletons get their own indicator (`.is_singleton_male`) and no member
contrast (their `.member_contrast_arbitrary` is 0). The `gmc` columns are
centered on everyone's support scores before the zeros are set. The print
also suggests the fixed-effect terms for the two-part partner predictor.

### Fit the model

With `family = gaussian()` and `dispformula = ~ 0`, the random effects
represent the residual covariance, as in the APIM vignette. Each row then
needs a random-effects term that covers it. Here, the shared and
member-contrast terms cover dyad members, and `.is_singleton_male` gives
singletons their own residual variance:

```{r dyad-solo-separate, eval = has_glmmTMB}
mm_separate <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  closeness ~ 1 + .partner_exists +
    .provided_support_gmc_actor + .provided_support_gmc_partner +
    (0 + .is_singleton_male | coupleID) +
    (0 + .is_exchangeable | coupleID) +
    (0 + .member_contrast_arbitrary | coupleID),
  family = gaussian(), dispformula = ~ 0,
  data = mm_data
)

nobs(mm_separate)
glmmTMB::fixef(mm_separate)$cond
```

All 200 people remain in the fit: 160 dyad members and 40 singletons. The
slopes can be compared with the simulated 0.6 and 0.3. Here,
`1 + .partner_exists` is the same as `0 + .is_exchangeable + .is_singleton_male`,
because every dyad member has a partner and no singleton has one.

Slopes are shared unless the model separates them. To let the actor slope
differ by partner status, add `.partner_exists:.provided_support_gmc_actor`.
In models with role-specific slopes, such as `.is_male:x`, singletons share
their role's slope through `I(.is_male + .is_singleton_male):x`.

### Residual variance of singletons: own or pooled

Let $a$ and $b$ be the variances of the shared and member-contrast terms. The
residual covariance of dyad members and the residual variance of singletons
are:

$$
R_{\mathrm{dyad}} =
\begin{pmatrix}a+b & a-b \\ a-b & a+b\end{pmatrix},
\qquad R_{\mathrm{singleton}} =
\begin{cases}
[\tau^2], & \text{own variance (model above)}, \\
[a+b], & \text{pooled}.
\end{cases}
$$

To pool, add the singleton indicator to **both** terms, so that both variance
components apply to everyone:

```{r dyad-solo-pooled, eval = has_glmmTMB}
mm_pooled <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  closeness ~ 1 + .partner_exists +
    .provided_support_gmc_actor + .provided_support_gmc_partner +
    (0 + I(.is_exchangeable + .is_singleton_male) | coupleID) +
    (0 + I(.member_contrast_arbitrary + .is_singleton_male) | coupleID),
  family = gaussian(), dispformula = ~ 0,
  data = mm_data,
  # Non-default settings help this example converge.
  control = glmmTMB::glmmTMBControl(
    optimizer = stats::optim,
    optArgs = list(method = "BFGS")
  )
)

recover_exchangeable_covariance(mm_pooled)
```

In this model, everyone has residual variance $a+b$, so the recovered member
variance also describes singletons. Only complete dyads identify the partner
covariance $a-b$, but pooling can change its estimate through the shared
parameters.

If the singleton indicator is added to the shared term only, singletons get
variance $a$ while dyad members keep $a+b$, and `recover_exchangeable_covariance()` stops with an error. The
same happens with the shared term `us(1 | coupleID)` of the APIM vignette and
a plain contrast term. An intercept already covers every row, so with
`(1 | coupleID)` add the singleton indicator to the contrast term only:
`(0 + I(.member_contrast_arbitrary + .is_singleton_male) | coupleID)`. This
gives the same model as `mm_pooled`, as long as all rows are male-male dyad
members or singleton men.

For female-male dyads, each role has its own variance. Singletons can share
the variance of their role. Fixed intercepts for each group already separate
rows with and without a partner, so `.partner_exists` is not needed:

```{r dyad-solo-distinguishable, eval = has_glmmTMB, message = FALSE}
fm_data <- prepare_dyad_data(
  fm_raw, dyad = coupleID, member = personID, role = gender,
  predictors = provided_support, add_apim_gmc_predictors = TRUE,
  partner_exists = has_partner == 1, seed = 123
)

fm_pooled <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  closeness ~ 0 + .is_male + .is_female +
    .is_singleton_male + .is_singleton_female +
    .provided_support_gmc_actor + .provided_support_gmc_partner +
    (0 + I(.is_male + .is_singleton_male) +
       I(.is_female + .is_singleton_female) | coupleID),
  family = gaussian(), dispformula = ~ 0,
  data = fm_data
)
```

For separate singleton variances, use
`(0 + .is_singleton_male | coupleID) + (0 + .is_singleton_female | coupleID)`
next to `(0 + .is_male + .is_female | coupleID)`. In both cases, the partner
covariance comes from complete dyads only. Pooling does not create covariance
between unrelated singletons.

A pooled model is a restricted version of the separate one, so a
likelihood-ratio test compares them. Test with the final fixed effects,
because predictors left out add unexplained variance to some groups only
(here, partner support to dyad members):

```{r dyad-solo-pooling-test, eval = has_glmmTMB}
compare_nested_models(mm_pooled, mm_separate)
```

A non-significant test does not show that the variances are equal. Pool when
equal residual variances are plausible on substantive grounds. With separate
singleton variances, only the shared fixed effects link singleton and dyad
estimates.

## Longitudinal data: losing or gaining a partner

Without `partner_exists`, a partner who has no row at an occasion is treated
as existing, with missing values. After a death, the survivor's later rows
then drop out of models with momentary partner predictors. With
`partner_exists`, these rows are kept with two-part predictors.

With `time`, `prepare_dyad_data()` splits each predictor into a momentary
deviation from the person's usual level (`cwp`) and the usual level itself
(`cbp`), so that within-person changes and between-person differences get
separate slopes [@curranDisaggregationWithinBetween2011]. See the
[intensive longitudinal APIMs](apim.html#intensive-longitudinal-apims).

### Example: a partner dies

Anna and Ben take part in a panel study. Ben dies after wave 3. In the
timeline, ● is a row with data:

| wave | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anna | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Ben | ● | ● | ● | | |
| `partnered` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` |

If the data file has empty rows for Ben after his death, remove them.
Otherwise, they count as occasions without a partner when Ben's share of
occasions with a partner (`.partner_exists_cbp`) is computed.

The simulated `panel` also contains a couple that stays together and a
couple that separates after wave 3 (both keep taking part). `partnered`
records relationship status:

```{r simulate-panel, include = FALSE}
set.seed(20261014)
panel <- expand.grid(wave = 1:5, member = 1:2, coupleID = 1:3) |>
  mutate(
    personID = c("Cleo", "Dan", "Anna", "Ben", "Eva", "Finn")[
      (coupleID - 1) * 2 + member
    ],
    partnered = !(coupleID %in% 2:3 & wave >= 4),
    health = round(rnorm(n(), 5, 1), 1),
    wellbeing = round(rnorm(n(), 5, 1), 1),
    satisfaction = if_else(partnered, round(rnorm(n(), 4, 1), 1), NA_real_)
  ) |>
  filter(!(personID == "Ben" & wave >= 4)) |>
  select(coupleID, personID, wave, partnered, health, satisfaction, wellbeing)
```

```{r prepare-panel}
prepared <- prepare_dyad_data(
  panel, dyad = coupleID, member = personID, time = wave,
  predictors = health, lag1_predictors = health,
  partner_exists = partnered, seed = 1
)
```

The message lists the suggested terms. Anna's rows show the coding of Ben's
health:

```{r panel-anna-rows}
prepared |>
  filter(personID == "Anna") |>
  select(
    wave, .partner_exists, .partner_exists_lag1,
    .health_cwp_partner, .health_cwp_partner_lag1,
    .health_cbp_partner_when_exists, .health_cbp_partner_after_exists
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

- From wave 4, `.partner_exists` is 0, and Ben's momentary deviation
  (`.health_cwp_partner`) is 0 in Anna's rows.
- Ben's usual level moves from `_when_exists` to `_after_exists`. Setting it
  to 0 would assume that it no longer relates to Anna's outcome. In its own
  column, it gets its own slope.
- At wave 4, the lagged value still holds Ben's wave-3 value. It pairs with
  `.partner_exists_lag1`, which is 1 there.
- `.partner_exists_cwp` and `.partner_exists_cbp` (not shown) split the
  status into losing or gaining a partner (within person) and the share of
  occasions with a partner (between persons). Use both instead of
  `.partner_exists`.

A model with the suggested terms (random effects kept minimal here):

```{r panel-model, eval = FALSE}
glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  wellbeing ~ 1 + .partner_exists_cwp + .partner_exists_cbp +
    .partner_exists_lag1 +
    .health_cwp_actor + .health_cbp_actor +
    .health_cwp_partner + .health_cwp_partner_lag1 +
    .health_cbp_partner_when_exists + .health_cbp_partner_after_exists +
    (1 | coupleID / personID),
  data = prepared
)
```

The section "People observed without their partner" in
`?prepare_dyad_data` explains how to interpret these coefficients.

### Separation, new relationships, and on-off relationships

| wave | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Separation (both keep taking part) | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` |
| New relationship (partner joins at wave 3) | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` |
| On-off relationship | `TRUE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` |

- **Separation.** The preparation and model are as for a death, and both
  keep their rows. The former partner's usual level includes their
  occasions after the separation.
- **New relationship.** Before the relationship, the partner's usual level
  is in `_before_exists`. It can relate to the outcome through selection
  (who ends up together). If the data also contain losses,
  `.partner_before_exists` is added, so that occasions before a relationship
  and after a loss get their own means.
- **On-off relationship.** A partner who returns is treated as the same
  partner, with a message. The gap counts as after a relationship
  (`_after_exists`). A different partner is not supported. End the person's
  data before the relationship with the different partner.

Splitting the usual level into before and after needs a numeric `time`.
Otherwise, it is not split, with a warning.

## Actor variables that exist only with a partner

Some of a person's own variables exist only with a partner, for example
ratings of the partner or of the relationship. They are missing where no
partner exists, so these rows drop out of models that use them.
`prepare_dyad_data()` applies two-part coding to partner predictors only,
but you can apply it to such actor variables after preparing the data.

In cross-sectional data, or when the status never changes within a dyad,
set the actor columns to 0 where `.partner_exists` is 0, for example with
`if_else(.partner_exists == 0, 0, .x_gmc_actor)`. Use `dplyr::if_else()`,
because multiplying by `.partner_exists` keeps missing values (`0 * NA` is
`NA`).

When the status changes, also split the actor's usual level by partner
status, as `prepare_dyad_data()` does for partner predictors. In `panel`,
`satisfaction` is a relationship rating that is missing where no partner
exists:

```{r actor-two-part, message = FALSE}
prepared <- prepare_dyad_data(
  panel, dyad = coupleID, member = personID, time = wave,
  predictors = c(health, satisfaction), lag1_predictors = satisfaction,
  partner_exists = partnered, seed = 1
) |>
  mutate(
    # First wave with a partner in the couple (Inf if never).
    first_partnered = if (any(.partner_exists == 1)) {
      min(wave[.partner_exists == 1])
    } else {
      Inf
    },
    .by = coupleID
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Momentary part: 0 where no partner exists (at this or the previous wave).
    .satisfaction_cwp_actor = if_else(
      .partner_exists == 0, 0, .satisfaction_cwp_actor
    ),
    .satisfaction_cwp_actor_lag1 = if_else(
      .partner_exists_lag1 %in% 0, 0, .satisfaction_cwp_actor_lag1
    ),
    # Usual level, split by partner status.
    .satisfaction_cbp_actor_when_exists = if_else(
      .partner_exists == 1, .satisfaction_cbp_actor, 0
    ),
    .satisfaction_cbp_actor_before_exists = if_else(
      .partner_exists == 0 & wave < first_partnered & is.finite(first_partnered),
      .satisfaction_cbp_actor, 0
    ),
    .satisfaction_cbp_actor_after_exists = if_else(
      .partner_exists == 0 & wave > first_partnered,
      .satisfaction_cbp_actor, 0
    )
  )

prepared |>
  filter(personID == "Anna") |>
  select(
    wave, satisfaction, .satisfaction_cwp_actor,
    .satisfaction_cbp_actor_when_exists, .satisfaction_cbp_actor_after_exists
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Use the recoded `.satisfaction_cwp_actor` and `.satisfaction_cwp_actor_lag1`,
and the split columns in place of `.satisfaction_cbp_actor`, together with
the status terms that `prepare_dyad_data()` suggests. Leave out a split
column that is 0 everywhere (here `_before_exists`, because no relationship
begins in these data). Rows of couples or singletons without a partner at
any occasion are 0 in all these columns, so they need their own fixed
intercept, such as singleton indicators.

`.partner_exists_lag1` is only created with lagged predictors and when the
status differs from the previous occasion somewhere. Otherwise, compute the same status with
`partner_exists_lag1 = .partner_exists[match(wave - 1, wave)]` and
`.by = coupleID`.
